prayer.text: Saint Martin de Porres, pray for us.

cues.text: Born Into Rejection
Martin de Porres Velázquez was born in Lima, Peru, on December 9, 1579.
His father was a Spanish nobleman, Juan de Porres, and his mother was Ana, a freed slave from Panama.
After his father abandoned the family, Martin, his mother, and his younger sister lived in poverty.
When Martin was twelve, his mother apprenticed him to a barber-surgeon.
There he learned to cut hair, draw blood, care for wounds, and prepare and give medicines, and the work helped him support his family.
Barred by the Law
Martin felt called to something more, and he asked the Dominican priory of the Holy Rosary in Lima to take him in as a lay helper.
The law in Peru, however, prohibited descendants of Africans and Indians from joining religious orders.
So Martin entered as a servant.
He cut the friars' hair, scrubbed floors, swept, and tended to the poor, doing the humblest work in the house.
A Law Quietly Set Aside
The prior, Juan de Lorenzana, had seen the depth of Martin's prayer and charity and his skill with the sick.
When Martin was twenty-four, the prior decided to ignore the law.
In 1603 Martin professed vows as a Dominican lay brother, a rank the Order now calls a cooperator brother.
Not every friar welcomed it, and some were cruel to him.
Once the priory fell into debt, and the prior meant to sell some of its valuables.
Martin offered himself instead, telling his brothers he was only a poor mulatto and they could sell him.
A Healer for the Whole City
Martin was placed in charge of the infirmary, where he cared for the sick and elderly friars.
In his spare time he also tended the sick outside the priory, nobles and slaves alike.
He treated everyone the same, whatever their color, race, or station.
He founded an orphanage and ministered to the African slaves brought to Lima.
He managed the priory's daily alms with both practicality and generosity, and he raised money for dowries so that poor girls could marry or enter a convent.

Those who knew him reported ecstasies in which he was lifted into the air, light filling the room where he prayed, bilocation, miraculous knowledge, instantaneous cures, and a remarkable rapport with animals.
Many of his fellow religious came to him for spiritual direction, yet Martin kept calling himself a "poor slave."
Friends in Lima
Martin was a good friend of St. Rose of Lima , a lay Dominican who respected his penances and labors.
He was also close to St. Juan Macías, a fellow Dominican lay brother.
Legacy
In January 1639 Martin fell gravely ill with chills, fevers, and tremors.
After almost a year of suffering, he died in the Rosary Convent on November 3, 1639, at the age of fifty-nine.
As he lay dying, the viceroy, the Count of Chinchón, knelt by his bed and asked his blessing.
Twenty-five years later his body was exhumed and found intact, giving off a sweet fragrance.
Pope Gregory XVI beatified him on October 29, 1837, and Pope John XXIII canonized him on May 6, 1962.
He is the patron of interracial justice, people of mixed race, barbers, innkeepers, and public health workers.
Vatican News describes a heart that followed the precept of charity, loving God and neighbor with a single, undivided love.
A law could keep him out of the habit for years, but it could not keep him from loving his neighbor.
We ask his prayers for every place where people are still divided by the color of their skin.
